clue.text: Like a mother bird swallowed by heartless mammal

indicators.note: To be swallowed is to go down inside the thing doing the swallowing, so one word sits in the middle of the other.
Heartless is without a heart, and a word's heart is the pair of letters at its dead centre.

parts.note: MAMMAL with the MM at its centre cut away
a tern is the sea bird every setter keeps in the drawer

explanation.walkthrough: The word being operated on is 'mammal' itself, which is why nothing in the clue names a particular beast — and the bird ends up inside the mammal rather than the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a mother → MATERNAL: maternal is the adjective for anything belonging to a mother, from instinct to the grandmother on that side.

clue.text: Flexible English isle up to support shopping complex

indicators.note: In a down entry up runs from the bottom of the grid towards the top, so the island is read the other way round.
To support a thing is to stand beneath it, so this piece is written under the one it holds up.

parts.note: Elba, Napoleon's isle, climbing the grid
E is the usual one-letter abbreviation for English
a mall is the covered shopping complex

explanation.walkthrough: Elba is the crossword's standard small island, and it is doing double duty here: the surface wants a holiday brochure while the letters want a staircase.
explanation.definitionFit: Flexible → MALLEABLE: a malleable metal can be hammered into a new shape, and the word carries the same sense of a person who bends under pressure.

clue.text: Swimmer clipped part of motor

indicators.note: Something clipped has had its end trimmed off, so the last letter never reaches the grid.

parts.note: a turbot is a large flatfish, and a fish is a swimmer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' is one of those deliberately vague nouns — athlete, fish or bird — and the enumeration is what tells you which. Trim the fish and the engine part is left.
explanation.definitionFit: part of motor → TURBO: the turbo is the turbocharger bolted to an engine, so the definition names the answer as one component of the whole.

clue.text: Soldiers finished eating hot duck

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the army's sappers

indicators.note: Whatever is eaten goes inside the eater, so the single letter is swallowed by the word beside it.

parts.note: dead is finished in the most final sense
H is the hot tap and the hot setting on a dial

explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the cricketing nought or the verb for stooping, and is neither: the redhead is a North American diving bird.
explanation.definitionFit: duck → REDHEAD: the redhead is a diving duck of North America, named for the drake's coppery head, so the clue defines by species.

clue.text: Alto records wide range

definitions.note: The answer is a plural name for one single chain of mountains, so the singular 'range' fits the thing even though the word itself is plural.

parts.note: A is the score's abbreviation for the alto voice
LPs are long-playing records

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are music, which is what makes the mountains such a surprise — and LP for a record is a piece of vocabulary worth banking early.
explanation.definitionFit: wide range → ALPS: the Alps are Europe's great mountain chain, so 'range' defines by example and 'wide' merely measures it.

clue.text: Soft copper retiring

parts.note: Cu is copper on the periodic table
a retiring person is a shy one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' reads like an instruction to turn something round and is doing nothing of the sort — it is the plain adjective. 'Copper' is the metal, not the policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft → CUSHY: a cushy number is an easy, undemanding job, which is the colloquial sense of soft that means requiring no effort.

clue.text: Admit company head's squeezed head of finance

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation on every company's letterhead

indicators.note: Something squeezed is forced into a space that was not expecting it, so the letter goes in between the ones already written.

parts.note: a ness is a headland — Loch Ness, Sheerness, Inverness

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it begins with, so only finance's opening letter is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of finance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is used twice over and means something different each time: once a headland, once simply the letter a word starts with. Spot that and the boardroom surface falls away.
explanation.definitionFit: Admit → CONFESS: to confess is to admit a fault or a crime, the sense of admitting that concedes guilt rather than letting somebody in.

clue.text: Mired in kerfuffle punching cross superhero

indicators.note: punching means the jumbled letters break into the middle of the other word

parts.note: to span a river is to cross it, so span means cross

indicators.note: a kerfuffle is a commotion or fuss, so letters in one are tossed into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a commotion is lashing out angrily at a comic-book hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like an adjective for angry, but it is a verb, as a bridge crosses a river. 'in kerfuffle' scrambles MIRED and 'punching' drives that into the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Spider-Man is the Marvel comics character Peter Parker, who swings between buildings on webs.

clue.text: Give up gym, stripping to exercise topless

indicators.note: to joins the stripped letter on to what follows
stripping takes off the outer layers, leaving only the middle of gym

parts.note: its middle letter is Y

indicators.note: topless means losing the top, the first letter

parts.note: to wield power is to exercise it

explanation.surface: Someone quitting the gym because they would have to work out shirtless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripping' removes both ends of gym; 'topless' removes the first letter of WIELD.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to surrender or concede, which is giving up.

clue.text: Forgotten in Nice, a dilapidated rental

parts.note: un is the French for 'a', fitting the French city of Nice

indicators.note: dilapidated means falling apart, so the letters of the following word collapse into a new order

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker has forgotten about a run-down rented flat on the Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like the adjective but is the French city, telling you to put 'a' into French; 'dilapidated' then rearranges RENTAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unlearnt has been put out of mind, its learning lost or deliberately dropped.

clue.text: Sensational learner freed after university

indicators.note: After is about position rather than time: what it introduces has already been written down when the next piece arrives.

parts.note: L is the plate on a learner driver's car
U is the standard abbreviation for university
to be rid of something is to be freed of it

explanation.walkthrough: L for learner and U for university are two of the abbreviations a solver meets weekly — worth learning once and keeping for good.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensational → LURID: lurid means shocking in a garish, tabloid way, the sense of sensational that means designed to shock rather than excellent.

clue.text: Work on spike in sound machine's output

indicators.note: To work dough or clay is to push it into an entirely new shape, which is what the letters here are asked to do.

parts.note: the nine letters of ON SPIKE IN thoroughly worked over

explanation.walkthrough: 'Work on' reads as a single verb and is really an instruction plus the start of its own raw material, which is why the fodder is so hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: sound machine's output → PINK NOISE: sleep machines play white, brown or pink noise, pink being the deeper-toned hiss with the bass turned up.

clue.text: Last of hare sprang and ran off

indicators.note: Last of asks for the final letter alone, so the animal contributes its tail rather than the whole of itself.

parts.note: the last letter of hare
to lope is to run in long easy bounds

explanation.walkthrough: A single letter taken off an animal and a past tense taken whole — and the definition is the pair of words at the far end, where 'off' looks like part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: ran off → ELOPED: to elope is to run off with someone to marry in secret, so the plain phrase covers the answer's narrower romantic sense.

clue.text: Republican first lady to rip into minister

parts.note: R is the letter beside a Republican's name on a US ballot
Eve was the first lady of all, long before the White House
to rend cloth is to rip it

explanation.walkthrough: 'First lady' is the Book of Genesis, not the White House, and that single switch turns a story about American politics into one about the pulpit.
explanation.definitionFit: minister → REVEREND: used as a noun, a reverend is the clergyman who holds the title, so it names a minister of the church.

clue.text: Get on with photos, having secured right clothes

parts.note: to board a bus is to get on it

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast, and a letter held fast is one trapped in the middle of a word.

parts.note: a photographer's shots are photos
R is the map and stage abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: Both long pieces are everyday words hiding shorter synonyms: 'get on' is boarding rather than making progress, and 'photos' are shots rather than pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: clothes → BOARD SHORTS: board shorts are the long surfing trunks worn in the water, so 'clothes' names them by the broad category they belong to.

clue.text: A children's game run through immediately

parts.note: the clue's opening word, written down as the letter it is
tag is the playground chase every child knows
to lance is to run something through with a point

explanation.walkthrough: 'Run through' is a spear rather than a rehearsal, and the opening 'A' is a letter rather than an article — the two places this clue expects you to look straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: immediately → AT A GLANCE: something clear at a glance is taken in the instant you look at it, so the phrase means as soon as it is seen.

clue.text: Base fellow essentially mainlining wine

parts.note: a fellow is a he, one of the shortest synonyms in the game

indicators.note: Essentially asks for the essence of a word, the letters sitting at its dead centre and nothing on either side.

parts.note: the two letters at the middle of MAINLINING
port is the fortified wine passed to the left

explanation.walkthrough: 'Base fellow' reads as an insult, which is the trap — 'base' is a noun and belongs to the definition, while 'mainlining' is raw material rather than the drug reference it pretends to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Base → HELIPORT: a heliport is the base a helicopter operates from, so 'base' names it as the station where the aircraft is kept.

clue.text: Computer club loses backing

indicators.note: The backing of a word is its rear, so losing it means the final letter is dropped.

parts.note: a mace is a spiked club, and also the one a mayor carries

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loses backing' sounds like a sponsor walking away and is really a letter walking off the end. 'Club' is the weapon, not the nightspot.
explanation.definitionFit: Computer → MAC: Apple's Macintosh has been shortened to Mac for forty years, so the brand's nickname stands in for the machine itself.

clue.text: Scams nurse with suspicious agreement

parts.note: a con is a scam and a con artist runs one
EN is the enrolled nurse, a standing crossword shortening
sus is the British slang clipping of suspicious

explanation.walkthrough: Three shortenings in a row, and the middle one is the one to bank: EN for enrolled nurse turns up in these puzzles far more often than any nurse does.
explanation.definitionFit: agreement → CONSENSUS: a consensus is the general view a group settles on, the collective sense of agreement rather than a signed contract.

clue.text: Wild unclothed period

indicators.note: unclothed means stripped of the outer covering, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: feral means wild, as of an animal living untamed

explanation.surface: A naked, untamed spell of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unclothed' strips the outside letters from the word for wild, leaving its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a long, distinct period of history, such as the Victorian age.

clue.text: Spread, if melting over steak

indicators.note: to spread is to scatter things widely, so the letters are scattered into a fresh order

parts.note: over and on can share a sense, as with a blanket lying over or on a bed

explanation.surface: Butter melting over a steak is spread across it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' looks like butter or a topping, but it scatters the letters of IF MELTING; 'over' then adds ON at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Filet mignon is a tender cut of beef taken from the narrow end of the tenderloin.

clue.text: Loud band with extremely egregious haircuts

parts.note: f is forte, the score's instruction to play loud
a band round a finger or a barrel is a ring

indicators.note: Extremely points at the extremes of the word, the letter at each far end and nothing in between.

parts.note: the outermost letters of egregious

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud band' paints a rock group and neither word is musical in that way: one is the dynamic marking f, the other a plain metal hoop.
explanation.definitionFit: haircuts → FRINGES: a fringe is hair cut straight across the forehead, what Americans call bangs, so the definition names a style of cut.

clue.text: Current translation of Narnia from the Middle East

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current in physics

indicators.note: translation of turns the word into another form, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A new version of the Narnia books has been translated for readers in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective for up to date, but it is the physics symbol I; 'translation of' rearranges NARNIA, the land in C. S. Lewis's children's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Iranian describes a person or thing from Iran, a country in the Middle East.

clue.text: Muse about work, boring friends endlessly

indicators.note: Boring is drilling a hole through something, so whatever does it ends up buried in the middle.
Endlessly means without an end, so the final letter of the word never gets written down.

parts.note: c is circa, the abbreviation for about a date
allies are friends, and endlessly they give up their S
op is a composer's opus, a work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring friends' is the surface at its most inviting and neither word means what it seems: the friends are allies and the boring is a drill.
explanation.definitionFit: Muse → CALLIOPE: Calliope is the eldest of the nine Muses and the one who presides over epic poetry, so the general word is defined by one of them.

clue.text: Performer to share amplifier with another?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an entertainer who tells jokes on stage
second meaning, read cryptically: the prefix co- means jointly with another, and a mic is the microphone that amplifies a voice, so to have a joint mic

explanation.surface: A singer asks whether they will have to share the stage microphone with someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as a whimsical split of the word into a prefix meaning jointly and the short name for a microphone.
explanation.definitionFit: A comic is a comedian, an entertainer whose act consists of jokes and funny stories.

clue.text: To annoy deer, cut grass back

indicators.note: Something cut is made shorter, so the word gives up the letter at its end.
This entry runs across the grid, so back means reading the assembled letters from right to left.

parts.note: an elk is the largest of the deer
a nark is a police informer, one who grasses

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the informer of a police drama rather than the lawn a deer would be eating — the one word that has to leave the surface picture entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy → RANKLE: to rankle is to go on irritating, a slight that keeps stinging long after the moment it was given.

clue.text: Popular first pair of knickers to have

parts.note: the first two letters of knickers, a pair being two
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: Someone is keen to get their hands on a well-liked pair of underpants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pair' suggests a pair of knickers, but here it means two letters: the first two of the word. Knickers are British women's underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: Known means widely recognised or familiar, so a known figure is a popular one.

clue.text: Wee partridge's introduction?

parts.note: a wee is a pee, the nursery word for it

indicators.note: An introduction comes at the front, so the bird's name contributes only the letter it opens with.

parts.note: the letter Partridge begins with

explanation.walkthrough: Read it twice. Once every word is wordplay, and once the same words are a plain description — which is what an &lit is, and why the question mark is there.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the thin cheep a newly hatched partridge makes is its first announcement of itself.

clue.text: Pennsylvania city pursuing absurd new mega zoo

indicators.note: pursuing means following behind, so the city comes after the rearranged letters
absurd means nonsensical, so the letters are put into a senseless new order

parts.note: Erie is a city in Pennsylvania on the lake of the same name

explanation.surface: A Pennsylvania city chases a ridiculous new giant zoo project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new mega' looks like one stretch of anagram fodder, but 'new' supplies only its abbreviation before 'absurd' does its mixing; 'pursuing' then sends the city to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A menagerie is a collection of wild animals kept for exhibition, an old-fashioned word for a zoo.

clue.text: Decreases caddie's burden

definitions.meaning: split it after the two opening letters and it is de-creases, which is what a hot flat one does to a shirt
the numbered clubs a golfer's caddie hauls round eighteen holes

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions, no letters to assemble. The first is a word cut in an unexpected place, and once you see the cut the whole clue stops being about shrinking anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To de-crease a shirt is to press it; and a golfer's irons are the numbered clubs weighing down the caddie's bag.

clue.text: Starters of certain horizontal entries (seven) help around enclosing, striking the centre

definitions.text: Starters of certain horizontal entries (seven) help around enclosing, striking the centre

indicators.note: starters are the first letters of the words that follow

parts.note: their first letters are C, H, E and S

indicators.note: around means wrapping, so the call for help goes round the rest

parts.note: SOS is the distress call for help

indicators.note: striking out the centre removes the middle letter

parts.note: penning means enclosing, as sheep in a pen

explanation.surface: A puzzle note that seven across answers start with something, plus a cry for help around a fence.
explanation.walkthrough: Seven across answers begin with chess terms (MATE, PIN, BOARD, RANK, FILE, ELO, MEN), the theme the clue points to; 'Starters' does double duty as openings.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess openings are the first moves of a game, so they are its starters.
